newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE - Grains to pour down South America waterway.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Grains to pour down South America waterway.

text.p: South America's mighty rivers are being rehabilitated in a $700 million project which will make the region's grain exports even more competitive.

The five-nation Paraguay-Parana Hidrovia waterway project centres on broadening and dredging the Paraguay river, running through farmland in Brazil, Bolivia and Paraguay and out to the Atlantic through Argentina's Parana river.
The project, which also includes Uruguay, will bring South America's soybean heartlands in range of ocean-going vessels and reduce growers' needs for more expensive road transport.
The people of the vast region of southern South America have always used the rivers for transport.

Spanish conquistadores sailed down the river Paraguay and then into other rivers to reach Peru. There was a thriving traffic in cargo ships as recently as the 1950s. But the growing use of trucks and trains coupled with the beginning of a 25-year cycle of low waters to squeeze river traffic to a trickle. Maintenance, such as dredging, was neglected.
A new spirit of cooperation, and revitalised economies in South America in the 1980s, led the authorities to remember their great natural advantages in river transport.

"This globalisation of the economy and the growing importance of communications and transport has led the countries to look at the river again," said Jesus Gonzalez, the head of the Hidrovia project and Argentina's Undersecretary of Ports and Waterways.
SINKING COSTS
The Hidrovia, which includes substantial port improvements, is due to be completed in 1999, but exporters shipping soybeans from Brazil's Matto Grosso are already seeing their bottom line improve.

"When the programme began in 1988 or 1989, the cost per kilometre of transporting a tonne of soybeans, for example. was at 28 thousandths of a dollar. Now this is down and we are at between nine and 11 thousandths of a dollar per kilometre per tonne," Gonzalez told Reuters.

River traffic going south from Brazil through the waterway has soared from about 800,000-1.2 million tonnes a year in the late 1980s to 7.1 million tonnes in the first eight months of 1996, and a projected nine to 10 million tonnes in 1997.
"Once this is complete, we estimate that Brazil is going to ship about 11-15 million tonnes of grain cargo through the waterway, fundamentally soybeans," Gonzalez said.
ARGENTINE STRETCH ALMOST COMPLETE

Argentina aims to complete its part of the project this year. The government will announce contracts to dredge the waterway from the Argentine grain hub of Santa Fe to Paraguay's capital Asuncion and the entire Upper Parana up to Puerto Iguazu, Gonzalez said.
The new stretch will mean the waterway is 50 percent complete. Project members think it should cut the cost of transporting soybeans to seven thousands of a dollar.
"Our final objective is to make it to five thousandths of a dollar per kilometre per tonne of soybeans, and three thousandths of a dollar for iron ore," Gonzalez said.
About $400 million of the total $700 million cost of the project has already been spent, much of it by private companies granted concessions.

"This is a project with an extremely important economic impact but the investment in dredging and signals from Santa Fe to Corumba, which is 2,200 km (1,400 miles), is only $80 million," Gonzalez said.
ENVIRONMENTAL CONTROVERSY

The next stage of the Hidrovia is the most controversial, as it goes through Brazil's enormous Pantanal swamplands, the world's largest wetlands which shelter more than 150,000 species of animals and plants.

The project as originally conceived -- which was to have cost a total $1 billion and not have been completed until 2005 -- was to have deepened the waterway through the Pantanal. But it caused protests from environmentalists who said it could jeopardise the wildlife.
Plans for the waterway to be deepened through the Parana to allow the passage of 1,500-tonne barges were dropped and none larger than 500 tonnes will now make it into the Pantanal.
Gonzalez said the reduction in scale of the waterway should not affect most of the grains traffic, most of which is further downriver. Environmentalists should now lay their fears to rest, he said.

"We can't do anything which drains the Pantanal because then it would be useless for shipping. We can't do anything which increases the speed of the water because then boats couldn't sail down it," he said.
An area covering 280,000 square miles (725,000 square km) with a population of 40 million will be within useful distance of the Hidrovia, which has already begun to attract investment.

Bolivia's soybean output has grown to about a million tonnes from almost nothing in the late 1980s, when the country's only port with access to the sea was constructed on the Hidrovia. Last year, U.S. commodities giant Cargill announced a joint-venture to operate a soybean storage and handling elevator at Puerto Aguirre.
But Argentine exporters with eyes on Brazil are ensuring not all of the traffic through the Hidrovia is oceanbound.
"Wheat is already beginning to go by river, and they are experimenting with sending wheat by barge up to Corumba in Brazil and from Corumba by truck to Brasilia," Gonzalez said.
